a: There are no pangs in their dying;
t: "No pangs in their death", or "no pangs; sound..."
p: Dividing one Hebrew word in two gives "They have no pangs; sound and fat is their body."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Greek also has "in their death"
readings.en: for there are no pangs (or bonds) at their death
readings.plain: There are no pangs in their dying;

readings.w: A modern conjecture (noted in BHS; followed by several modern versions): לָמוֹ תָּם, no manuscript
readings.en: for they have no pangs; sound (and fat is their body)
readings.plain: They have no pangs at all;

why: The Hebrew as written makes sense: the wicked die easily, without a long painful illness, which ancient readers counted a blessing. The redivision gives a smoother pair of lines (with "sound and fat are their bodies" as the second), but no manuscript or ancient version has it.
b: With the conjecture the whole verse reads: "They have no pangs; their bodies are sound and fat."

a: Their eye looks out from fat
p: The Greek and Syriac read "their iniquity comes out as from fat", a difference of one letter.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: their eye goes out from fat
readings.plain: Their eye looks out from fat

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Syriac Peshitta
readings.orig: ἐξελεύσεται ὡς ἐκ στέατος ἡ ἀδικία αὐτῶν
readings.en: their injustice will come out as from fat
readings.plain: Their guilt oozes out from fat

why: The Greek seems to have read עֲוֺנָמוֹ ("their iniquity") for עֵינֵמוֹ ("their eye"): the letters yod and waw were easily confused. Many modern versions follow the Greek. The Hebrew picture of eyes peering out of a fat face is odd but vivid, and the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: when you get up
t: "When you rouse yourself", or "in your city"
p: The Greek and the Gallican Latin read "in your city".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (vowels as a short form of בְּהָעִיר, 'when rousing')
readings.en: when rousing (yourself)
readings.plain: when you get up

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (in civitate tua)
readings.en: in your city
readings.plain: in your city

why: The same Hebrew consonants serve both readings. "When you wake" continues the dream image of the first line, so the Masoretic reading fits better.

a: They burned up all of God's meeting places across the land.
p: The Greek makes the second line the enemy's own words: "Come, let us burn up all the feasts of God from the land."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: they burned all the meeting places of God in the land
readings.plain: They burned up all of God's meeting places across the land.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: δεῦτε καὶ κατακαύσωμεν πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: Come, and let us burn up all the feasts of God from the land
readings.plain: "Come, let us burn up all the feasts of God from the land."

why: The Greek read the verb as "let us burn" (a cohortative) and mo'ade as "feasts", which the word can mean. It also read the first line's ninam ("let us oppress them") as "their offspring", giving "their kindred together said...". The Hebrew is the base text and reads well.
b: Some Greek witnesses, and Jerome's Gallican Latin after them (quiescere faciamus), read καταπαύσωμεν, "let us make cease", which is where Brenton's English (1844) gets "abolish".

a: You fed it to a people, to the desert dwellers.
p: The Greek has "to the Ethiopian peoples". Some scholars correct the Hebrew to "to the sharks of the sea".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you give it as food to a people, to desert creatures (or dwellers)
readings.plain: You fed it to a people, to the desert dwellers.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: ἔδωκας αὐτὸν βρῶμα λαοῖς τοῖς Αἰθίοψιν
readings.en: you gave him as food to the Ethiopian peoples
readings.plain: You gave it as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.

readings.w: Modern conjecture: לְעַמְלְצֵי יָם, no manuscript
readings.en: to the sharks of the sea
readings.plain: You fed it to the sharks of the sea.

why: Tsiyyim are desert creatures or nomads (Isaiah 13:21); the Greek translator identified them with the Ethiopians, as it does in Psalm 72:9. The conjecture rests on a rare word and on no witness. The Hebrew picture of the monster's carcass left in the desert is strange but can be understood.

a: Do not give your turtledove's life to a wild animal;
t: Your dove, or a soul that praises you
p: The Greek read the same letters as "a soul that confesses you".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: do not give to the wild beast the life of your turtledove
readings.plain: Do not give your turtledove's life to a wild animal;

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: μὴ παραδῷς τοῖς θηρίοις ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι
readings.en: do not hand over to the wild beasts a soul that confesses you
readings.plain: Do not hand over to the wild beasts a soul that praises you;

why: The Greek read תּוֹדֶךָ ("praising you") for תּוֹרֶךָ ("your turtledove"): resh and dalet look almost the same. The Hebrew image of a defenseless dove before a beast fits the parallel "your poor ones".

a: and your name is close by.
t: Your name is near, or we call on your name
p: The Greek reads "and we will call on your name".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and your name is near
readings.plain: and your name is close by.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Syriac Peshitta
readings.en: and we will call on your name
readings.plain: and we will call on your name.

why: The Greek seems to have read a verb, qaro' ("call"), for qarov ("near"). Some modern scholars prefer it, since calling on God's name is a common pair with giving thanks (Psalm 105:1). The Hebrew makes good sense: God's name, his active presence, is close.

a: or speak arrogance with a stiff neck.
p: The Greek has "do not speak injustice against God", reading "against the Rock" for "with a neck".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: speak arrogance with a neck
readings.plain: or speak arrogance with a stiff neck.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: μὴ λαλεῖτε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀδικίαν
readings.en: do not speak injustice against God
readings.plain: or speak injustice against God.

why: The Greek read בְּצוּר, "against the Rock", a title of God, for בְצַוָּאר, "with a neck", and translated the title as "God". The Hebrew image of the stiff, arrogant neck fits the raised horn of the same verse.

a: I will keep speaking out for all time
p: The Greek has "I will rejoice forever".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: but I will declare forever
readings.plain: I will keep speaking out for all time

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγαλλιάσομαι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
readings.en: but I will rejoice forever
readings.plain: I will rejoice for all time

why: The difference is one letter (אגיד "I will declare" and אגיל "I will rejoice"). The Hebrew fits the psalm's theme of telling God's wonders (75:1).

a: A song.
p: The Greek title adds "about the Assyrian", linking the psalm to Sennacherib's defeat in 701 BC.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a song
readings.plain: A song.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.en: an ode regarding the Assyrian
readings.plain: A song about the Assyrian.

why: The Greek titles add historical notes to several psalms; they show how Jews in Egypt read the psalms in the 200s–100s BC, not what the Hebrew title said. See the note at 76:5.

a: His lair was in Salem
p: The Greek translated the name: "His place was made in peace."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and his lair (booth) was in Salem
readings.plain: His lair was in Salem

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγενήθη ἐν εἰρήνῃ ὁ τόπος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and his place was made in peace
readings.plain: His place was made in peace

why: The Greek has the same Hebrew; it translated the name Salem as the word "peace" (shalom). The parallel "his den in Zion" shows that a place name is meant.

a: glorious beyond the hills of prey.
t: Mountains of prey, or everlasting mountains
p: The Greek has "from the everlasting mountains".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: than the mountains of prey
readings.plain: glorious beyond the hills of prey.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.en: from the everlasting mountains
readings.plain: glorious beyond the everlasting hills.

why: The Greek may have read 'ad ("forever") for teref ("prey"), or guessed. "Mountains of prey" fits the lion picture of 76:2: God comes down from the hills where he hunted, leaving his enemies as spoil (76:5).

a: you will strap on what remains of the fury.
p: The Greek has "and the remnant of (angry) thought will keep festival for you".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the remainder of furies you will gird on
readings.plain: you will strap on what remains of the fury.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.en: and the remnant of (angry) thought will keep festival for you
readings.plain: and what remains of the fury will hold a feast for you.

why: The Greek read tachog ("will keep a feast") for tachgor ("will gird on"). Many modern scholars find the Greek easier; the Hebrew is the base text and can be read (see the note on the verse).

a: This is what wounds me:
p: The Greek reads: "Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my sickness (wound) is this
readings.plain: This is what wounds me:

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Gallican Psalter (nunc coepi)
readings.en: now I have begun
readings.plain: Now I have begun:

why: The Greek took challoti from hechel, "to begin". In Latin, "Nunc coepi" became a famous motto of beginning again in Christian spirituality. The Hebrew reading "my wound" suits the lament. Both versions read the second line as "the change of the right hand", the reading the Plain English Translation follows.

a: He gave over their cattle to the hail,
p: A few Hebrew manuscripts and Symmachus are reported to read "to the plague" (laddever) for "to the hail" (labbarad).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Greek (εἰς χάλαζαν)
readings.en: he delivered their cattle to the hail
readings.plain: He gave over their cattle to the hail,

readings.w: A few medieval Hebrew manuscripts and Symmachus (as reported in the BHS apparatus); adopted by many scholars
readings.en: to the plague
readings.plain: He gave over their cattle to the plague,

why: The great majority of witnesses, including the Greek, have "hail", which also fits Exodus 9:24–25, where the hail struck animals in the field. "Plague" would add the livestock plague of Exodus 9:6 and suit "fire-bolts" (Reshef) in the next line; the letters b and d are easily confused, so either could be the copying error.

a: its young women heard no wedding praise.
p: The Greek has "its young women were not mourned".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and its young women were not praised (in wedding songs)
readings.plain: its young women heard no wedding praise.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: καὶ αἱ παρθένοι αὐτῶν οὐκ ἐπενθήθησαν
readings.en: and their maidens were not mourned
readings.plain: its young women were not mourned.

why: The Greek seems to have read a form of yalal, "wail", for halal, "praise". The Hebrew, with weddings that never happened, gives a sharper picture and matches Jeremiah's silenced wedding songs (Jeremiah 7:34).

a: for they have eaten Jacob up
p: The Masoretic Text has a singular verb; the Greek, the Syriac, several Hebrew manuscripts and Jeremiah 10:25 have the plural.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for he (it) has eaten Jacob
readings.plain: for it has eaten Jacob up

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Syriac Peshitta; several Hebrew manuscripts (as reported); Jeremiah 10:25
readings.en: for they have devoured Jacob
readings.plain: for they have eaten Jacob up

why: The plural matches the "nations" and "kingdoms" of 79:6 and the parallel in Jeremiah 10:25. The singular of the Masoretic Text can also be read as a collective ("each of them"), so the sense is the same either way; the Plain English Translation uses the plural.

a: A psalm.
p: The Greek title adds "about the Assyrian".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a psalm
readings.plain: A psalm.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.en: a psalm concerning the Assyrian
readings.plain: A psalm about the Assyrian.

why: As in 76:0, the Greek note records an early reading of the psalm against the Assyrian attacks on the northern tribes (see the note at 80:2). It is not in the Hebrew.

a: and our enemies mock among themselves.
t: Mock among themselves, or mock us
p: The Greek has "and our enemies mocked us".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and our enemies mock for themselves (or at them)
readings.plain: and our enemies mock among themselves.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931); Syriac Peshitta
readings.orig: καὶ οἱ ἐχθροὶ ἡμῶν ἐμυκτήρισαν ἡμᾶς
readings.en: and our enemies mocked us
readings.plain: and our enemies mock us.

why: The Greek seems to have read לָנוּ, "at us", for לָמוֹ. Many versions follow it. The Hebrew "among themselves" pictures the enemies laughing together, and the sense is close either way.

a: and the son you made strong for yourself.
p: The Greek has "son of man" here, as in 80:17.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and over the son (branch) you made strong for yourself
readings.plain: and the son you made strong for yourself.

readings.w: Septuagint, Old Greek Psalms (Rahlfs, Psalmi cum Odis, 1931)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπὶ υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου ὃν ἐκραταίωσας σεαυτῷ
readings.en: and over the son of man whom you made strong for yourself
readings.plain: and the son of man you made strong for yourself.

why: The Greek probably filled out the line from 80:17. The Hebrew "son" fits the vine picture (a son as a branch, Genesis 49:22). Many scholars think the whole line in the Hebrew was itself copied from 80:17 (see the note).
